group.passage:
Some 13.8 billion years ago, the universe began with a rapid expansion known as the Big Bang. The expansion later slowed down, allowing galaxies and stars to form. But around nine billion years after the Big Bang, the expansion began to speed up again, driven by a mysterious and invisible force now known as dark energy.
[[1]] Its existence wasn’t even discovered until 1998, and before that, the very idea of a growing universe was still relatively new.
In fact, Albert Einstein once believed the universe was static, not expanding at all. He introduced a concept called the cosmological constant—a kind of repulsive force that would balance gravity and keep the universe stable. But in 1929, the once popular assumption was disproved.
Astronomers Edwin Hubble and Milton Humason made a groundbreaking observation using Cepheid stars in distant galaxies to measure how far away those galaxies were. The duo then compared those distances with redshift—the phenomenon where light an object emits shifts towards the red end of the spectrum. [[2]] This was conclusive proof that the universe was expanding, with galaxies moving farther apart over time.
But the biggest surprise came in 1998, when two separate teams of astronomers made another key discovery. [[3]] Studying the brightness of distant supernovae—exploding stars that emit a consistent amount of light, the teams challenged the mainstream thinking. If the expansion of the universe were slowing down, these stars should have appeared brighter than expected. Instead, they appeared dimmer—a clear sign that the expansion was actually quickening. [[4]]
With its exact nature unknown, dark energy now stands as one of the most profound mysteries in modern cosmology.

options_bank.A: What they found was striking: the farther away a galaxy was, the greater its redshift, meaning it was moving faster.
options_bank.B: At that time, most believed that the universe’s expansion should be slowing down.
options_bank.C: The unexpected result pointed to the existence of dark energy, a powerful force pushing the universe apart at an increasing rate.
options_bank.D: Even today, scientists know very little about dark energy, despite the fact that it makes up about 70% of the universe.
options_bank.E: For a better illustration, we can think of galaxies in an expanding universe as raisins in a baking cake. As the dough rises, the raisins are carried farther apart.
